newsitem.title: ISRAEL: NorTel buys 20 percent of Koor's Telrad.
newsitem.headline: NorTel buys 20 percent of Koor's Telrad.

text.p: Canada's NorTel on Tuesday completed its purchase of 20 percent of Koor's Telrad unit for $45 million and Koor president Benjamin Gaon said he now planned to take Telrad public as soon as possible.

"The key reason why we were interested in making an investment in Telrad was because of its engineering and technical capabilities," Jean Monty, NorTel president and chief executive officer, said at a signing ceremony in Tel Aviv.

"We want to globalise and want to expand the product line of the company beyond its traditional roots. We're focusing heavily on mobility systems -- wireless systems," Monty told reporters at Koor headquarters.
Nortel, formerly Northern Telecom Ltd, designs, builds and integrates digital communications networks for information, entertainment, education and business.

It will pay $17.5 million in cash and another $27.5 million over four payments carrying interest of Libor plus 1/8 percent for 20 percent of Telrad Telecommunications and Electronic Industries Ltd, Israel's largest telecommunications equipment maker.

Nortel's holding will be in newly issued shares and will leave Koor, Israel's biggest holding company, with the remaining 80 percent. Koor also controls Tadiran Ltd, another telecom equipment maker. Nortel signed the two-year option agreement in January 1995.
Gaon said the deal was part of Koor's corporate strategy to link up with a leading multinational in each of its core businesses.
He said there was "keen interest" by both parties to take Telrad public.

"There's no date yet set. The idea is to make it as early as possible and I believe that since the Israeli capital market and the stock market is a sleeping beauty, we would prefer to have it out of Israel, probably in the United States," he said in English.
"By the time we'll be ready and you'll accept -- being now members of the board -- then we will be more than delighted to do it," he said, addressing Monty and other NorTel executives at the signing.
Monty said NorTel did not envision taking a larger stake in Telrad in the short term and sought research and development benefits rather than control.

Bezalel Levin, Telrad's president and CEO, told reporters the Israeli firm had won international tenders in the last six months for projects in Papua New Guinea, Bolivia and Georgia and was about to sign a deal in Ethiopia.

"This transaction (with NorTel) enhances our competitive ability to supply world class systems to (Israel's) Cellcom, Barak and Golden Lines, as well as our largest customer -- the Bezeq Telecommunications company -- and to expand our exports," he said.

Telrad had sales of $396 million in 1995. The Israeli company already has a strategic partnership with NorTel, under which it produces equipment under the NorTel name. It also sells its products independently.
Nortel had revenues of $12.85 billion in 1996, a 20 percent increase over 1995. Net earnings applicable to common shares for 1996 were $619 million, compared with $169 million.
